start.text: She stops for you again, and waits for you to be out of her way.

first.text: She stops when you step onto the path, the way you'd stop for a cart, and waits for you to be out of her way.

Close to, she's older than the Provost, and taller. The grey on her robe isn't dirt: it's the fog's, gone into the weave the way it goes into the Unmoored's, all the way up to the shoulders. Only the yoke and the hood are still white. There's a darker diamond on her breast where something stitched has been picked out.
You're in the way. I don't mind. Nobody's been in the way in a long time.
She looks at the ember in your hand. Not away from it, the way the Unmoored do. At it, a long time.
Somebody asked to carry one of those, once. I can't think who. I put that down with the rest.

choice.text: There's a boat in the boathouse at the Boat Stair. In the eighth slip.
Walk on. I'll get out of your way.

who.text: She stops, the way you stop at a stair that isn't there.

I came down out of there with something in my hands. Heavy. I carried it out on the moor in the dark and set it down, and in the morning it was gone. Not lost. Ness says that, doesn't she? Gone. I found that out before Ness did.
I don't miss it. You can't miss a thing you don't know the shape of. You only walk round.

why.text: She looks past you at the east stair door, open a hand's width on the dark.
If I stop, I'll go in. I don't know why I'd go in. But my feet know the way up, and they want it, so I keep them busy.
Round's a good shape. It doesn't go anywhere.

boat.text: Kept back, the warden's list says. On somebody's word.
Then somebody meant to go down in it, and didn't. I hope they had a reason. I hope it was a good one. It's a long way to swim.
Her hands open a little at her sides, and close again, as if they'd had oars in them.

know.text: It isn't a question. Down by the niche the chapter stands not watching, the way Keepers don't. The Provost has her back turned on purpose.
You've read her last page in the Spire's own book. Starved, not snuffed. One coal kept back. Signed in full, the way you'd sign a thing you meant somebody to find.

choice.text: Tell her: her name, and what she did, and why.
Ask her first whether she wants it back.
Say nothing. Step off the path and let her walk.

told.text: Your name is Oriel Sayre. You were the High Keeper. You put the Firstflame out.

There's a book under the Spire. Nine hundred midwinters of the Hushed, given to the flame with everything that was in them. You read it to the first page, and you starved the flame on purpose so it would all come home. You wrote it down and signed it.
She says it like somebody trying a key in a door. It turns.
Did I mean it? What I wrote.
You wrote: I will not choose for them again. Nobody chose that I should.
For a long while she doesn't say anything. Then she sits down where she is, on one of the old edge-stones beside the path, the way your legs fold at the end of a long day's walking.
Then I meant it. I'd know my own reasons. Even without them.
It's heavy. I'd forgotten that as well. That'll be why I put it down.
The Provost comes up the slope then. She doesn't hurry. She stands on the path, which nobody else has stood on.
Agathe. ...You'd be Agathe. I wrote to you.

asked.text: There's a book under the Spire with your name in it, and what you did, and why. Do you want it back?
She looks at you as if you'd held something out to her and then stepped back, and left her to take it or not.
Nobody's asked me anything in— I don't know how long. That's how long.
Then not yet. Not while I'm walking. I'd drop it.
Go up that stair first, whoever you are. If there's anything at the top worth coming back down for, come and ask me again. I'll want it then.
She steps round you, carefully, and walks on. Going past the door she doesn't look at it, but her pace is a little slower there than it was.

kept.text: Kind. Or careful. I can't tell those apart any more. I think I used to be able to.
She walks on round. Past the door, not looking.

bye.text: Thank you. Mind the door. It draws.

after_told.text: Oriel Sayre sits on the edge-stone by the path with her hands open on her knees, facing the east stair door.
Three names, last midwinter. I wrote them in for the giving, and gave nothing. I remember writing them now. I don't remember their faces. I hope that's the right way round.
I'm not walking round any more. I don't need to. I know why I'd go in, now. And I won't. That's somebody else's stair.
She's been singing since I sat down. I think she always was. I walked too loud to hear her.
You've been up the stair. She looks at your hood, pushed back, and then at the ember, and then away, out at the fog wall.
Somebody came down that stair counting. I heard it from here. I used to know a sound like that.

choice.text: It was me you gave it to. On the last landing.

after_asked.text: She stops for you, and waits for you to be out of her way.
Not yet. You said you'd go up first.
Somebody's singing on that stair. I walk past it. I think I always walked past it.
You've been up the stair. She looks at your hood, pushed back, and then at the ember, and then away, out at the fog wall.
You came down. I heard you counting. ...I said I'd want it, then. I'm not sure I'm brave enough. Not today. Ask me again.

choice.text: You said to ask you again when I came down. I'm asking.

after_kept.text: She stops for you, and waits for you to be out of her way.
You're in the way again. I don't mind.
Somebody's singing on that stair. I walk past it. I think I always walked past it.
You've been up the stair. She looks at your hood, pushed back, and then at the ember, and then away, out at the fog wall.
Somebody came down that stair counting. I walked faster. I don't know why.

choice.text: Somebody asked to carry one of those, you said. You gave it them.

asked_again.text: She stops walking. Not for you, this time. She stops the way a clock does when nobody's wound it.
Go on, then. Quickly, before I'm brave about it.

Your name is Oriel Sayre. You were the High Keeper. You read the Spire's book to its first page, and you starved the Firstflame on purpose so everything it ate would come home. You wrote it down, and signed it.
She tries it like a key in a door. It turns, and she puts a hand down on the nearest edge-stone, and sits, because her legs have decided to.
Heavy. You said it would be. You didn't say it would fit.

kept_told.text: Did I? Then I had one to give.
She looks up the Spire, all the way, to the dark of the lantern room under the cap; and then at the ember in your hand; and then she stops walking.
Nobody has a coal like that but whoever keeps the flame. So that's who I was. I wondered why the door kept drawing.
Don't tell me my name yet. Tell me who I gave it to. I'd like them in that order. I think I owe it that order.

novice.text: On the last landing, the night you put it out, a novice came up past the third notch because they'd heard somebody go up alone. They asked you for the last coal. It was me.

She looks at the ember first. Then at your hood, pushed back. Then at your face, a long time, the way the Provost looked at the foot of the stair; except that she's looking for something, and the Provost wasn't.
I pinned that hood. So nobody would see your face on that stair tonight. ...I didn't think I'd be one of the nobody.
You were so young. You said 'I can count' as if that were a thing to bring to a fire.
It was. It's all I got to the bottom with.
And then I went down to the niche with Aldous's knife and took you off the roll. I remember the sound of it. I remember that and not your face.
You've written it back. I saw Agathe stop at the niche and read something and not say it aloud. That'll be you.
You've struck it. Good. Struck can still be read. Scraped can't. I knew that when I did it.
You left it scraped. ...Thank you. It's the one thing I did that night I'm sure of.
I gave the last of the Spire to a child and told them to forget me. And they came back up the hill with it, and stood in my way.
Nobody ever gave me back anything. I don't know where you put it.
Oriel Sayre. You were the High Keeper.
...Oriel. Yes. That's the right weight. I'd have known it was mine if I'd found it in the road.
Down at the niche step the Provost has turned round. She isn't pretending not to watch any more.
Agathe. It was one of yours.
I know. They told me at the foot of the stair.
...I see that now. I saw the face and didn't know it.
You're going up. The lantern room. I can see it on you, the way the ember leans. It used to lean like that in my hands, at the top of the year.
What do you want of me? Say it plain. I've had enough of careful.

choice.text: Come up with me. You were the last one in that room.
Your boat's still in the eighth slip. Merrit's kept her greased.
Nothing. I'm not going to choose for you.

climb.text: I said that was somebody else's stair.
She looks at the door a long while.
It is. It's yours. But I know where the lantern-room door sticks, and I know where the coal sat. I'll come up behind you and carry nothing and touch nothing.
If they ask for it up there, the ember, I'd like to be in the room. Somebody should be who knows what it cost.
She goes and stands by the east stair door, close enough to put her hand on the frame. She doesn't. Not yet.

boat_down.text: I'll not run in her. I've done running. Round and round.
But somebody should see the Spire from the water, whatever you do up there. From the islands' side, where everybody else will be looking from. I'll go down and sit in her, and wait.
I'll take her down. I said I'd grease the rollers. In case.
Thank you. I never did learn how they go. Somebody always did it for me. That was the trouble with everything.
She goes off down the road towards the long steps, not round. It's the first time in a season her feet have gone anywhere but round.

own.text: She hears her own line come back to her. You can see it land.
'I will not choose for them again.' ...Nobody's ever handed me that. I only ever gave it.
Then I'll stand at the foot with the chapter, where I should have stood. The hand goes up. The chapter stays at the foot.
Somebody ought to count you who knows how many landings there are. Agathe only learned it this week.
She goes down to the niche step and stands a pace behind the Provost, her hands folded the same way. The Provost doesn't look round. She moves over.

after_knows.text: Oriel Sayre stands by the east stair door, with her hand not quite on the frame.
When you're ready. Not before. I walked round the bottom of it a whole season; I can stand still at it a while.
It draws. It always drew. I used to think that was the wind.
Oriel Sayre stands just inside the lantern-room door, carrying nothing, touching nothing.
Thirty-one midwinters I fed it in this room. I never once looked at those panes from inside. I thought they were black because it was night.
They stood round me every year while I sang the rite. I sang at them. I thought it was the wind in the glass.
Oriel Sayre stands on the niche step a pace behind the Provost, her hands folded the same way.
We don't talk. We don't need to. We've read the same book, and we've each of us signed something.
Your name's on the roll beside me. I read it, and I don't say it. That's a Keeper's manners.
She's quieter. Isolde. Or I'm listening better.
I sat with the chapter and didn't choose. I didn't know a Keeper could. I thought it was the one thing we couldn't help.
Seven landings. Count them going up. It's the coming down that's hard, and you've done that.

after_boat.text: Oriel Sayre sits on the eighth boat's thwart, up in her slip, with the oars across her knees, getting the weight of them.
Hild says you lean back, not pull. Let the boat come to you. I'll have it by the time you're up.
Merrit came and looked at me a long time and said 'Eighth' and went back to his bollard. I think that's the most anybody's said to me since I got here.
Go on up. I'll be looking from the water, with everybody else.
